topic.title: Advanced Tense Aspect
topic.summary: Aspect choices distinguish completed, ongoing, repeated, and temporary states in nuanced contexts.

rules.title: Aspectual choice
rules.explanation: Choose simple, continuous, or perfect aspect according to the time span and viewpoint.
rules.example: She has been researching the issue for months.

rules.title: Stative and dynamic shifts
rules.explanation: Some normally stative verbs take a continuous form when they describe a temporary or active experience.
rules.example: I am thinking about your proposal.

questions.prompt: By next June, she ___ on the project for a year.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'will have been working' is the future perfect continuous, expressing an action that will be in progress up to a specific future time.
Incorrect: 'works' is simple present, not appropriate for a future continuous period.
Incorrect: 'worked' is simple past and does not project into the future.
Incorrect: 'is working' is present continuous and does not express a future perfect timeframe.

questions.prompt: I ___ what you mean now.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'am beginning to understand' uses the dynamic shift of a stative verb in continuous form to describe a gradual process.
Incorrect: 'begin to understand' is grammatically possible but lacks the dynamic shift emphasis on an ongoing process.
Incorrect: 'understood' is simple past and does not fit the present context.
Incorrect: 'have understood' is present perfect but does not capture the ongoing understanding process.

questions.prompt: The researchers ___ three trials so far.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'have completed' is the present perfect, expressing completed actions with present relevance.
Incorrect: 'complete' is simple present and does not indicate past actions.
Incorrect: 'were completing' is past continuous and suggests an incomplete past action.
Incorrect: 'have been completing' would suggest ongoing repetition rather than completed trials.

questions.prompt: She ___ unusually quiet today.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'is being' applies the stative-dynamic shift to describe temporary, unusual behaviour.
Incorrect: 'is' describes a permanent state rather than temporary behaviour.
Incorrect: 'has been' is present perfect but lacks the dynamic shift emphasis.
Incorrect: 'was being' is past tense and does not fit today's present context.

questions.prompt: He ___ the same route every morning this week.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'has been taking' is the present perfect continuous, expressing a repeated action over a period of time.
Incorrect: 'takes' is simple present but lacks the temporal connection to the week.
Incorrect: 'is taking' is present continuous but doesn't express the repeated nature.
Incorrect: 'had taken' is past perfect and does not connect to the present week.

questions.faultySentence: She works here since 2020.
questions.prompt: Correct the aspect error.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'has worked here since 2020' uses present perfect with 'since' to express an action that started in the past and continues to the present.
Incorrect: This repeats the original error.
Incorrect: 'from 2020' is not used with present perfect to indicate duration.
Incorrect: 'is working ... since' incorrectly combines present continuous with 'since'.

questions.faultySentence: I am knowing the answer now.
questions.prompt: Correct the stative verb misuse.
choices: I am knowing the answer now.
I have known the answer now.
I am known to know the answer now.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'I know' uses the simple present form of the stative verb correctly.
Incorrect: This repeats the original error.
Incorrect: 'have known' would imply that you've known it for some time, but 'now' suggests immediate knowledge.
Incorrect: This unnecessarily complicates the sentence.

questions.prompt: The team ___ (review) the evidence all afternoon.
questions.explanation: 'has been reviewing' is the present perfect continuous, expressing an activity continuing over a period up to the present.

questions.prompt: I ___ (think) about changing the design.
questions.explanation: 'am thinking' uses the continuous form of 'think' when it means 'considering' rather than 'believe'.

questions.prompt: They ___ (already / solve) the main problem.
questions.explanation: 'have already solved' uses the present perfect with 'already' to express a completed action with present relevance.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence using present perfect continuous.
questions.explanation: The perfect continuous combines duration with a present viewpoint.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence using a stative verb in continuous form.
questions.explanation: 'Consider' takes the continuous form here because it describes an active thought process.

topic.title: Complex Narrative Time
topic.summary: Narrative time is anchored with past perfect forms and controlled shifts into the historical present.

rules.title: Past-time anchoring
rules.explanation: Use past perfect to mark an event as earlier than another past reference point.
rules.example: By noon, the guests had already left.

rules.title: Historical present
rules.explanation: The present tense can make a past narrative vivid, especially in summaries and storytelling.
rules.example: In 1969, the mission reaches the moon.

questions.prompt: When the ambulance arrived, the patient ___ consciousness.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'had regained' is the past perfect, placing the regaining before the arrival.
Incorrect: 'regained' is simple past and does not show the earlier event.
Incorrect: 'has regained' is present perfect and does not anchor to past time.
Incorrect: 'was regaining' is past continuous and suggests incompletion.

questions.prompt: In the final scene, the detective ___ the hidden letter.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'finds' uses the historical present for vivid storytelling.
Incorrect: 'found' is simple past and lacks the vivid present effect.
Incorrect: 'has found' is present perfect and less suitable for scene description.
Incorrect: 'is finding' suggests an ongoing process rather than a narrative event.

questions.prompt: She realised that she ___ the wrong file.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'had opened' is the past perfect, showing the file-opening happened before the realising.
Incorrect: 'opened' is simple past and does not indicate the order clearly.
Incorrect: 'has opened' is present perfect and does not anchor to past time.
Incorrect: 'was opening' suggests an ongoing action, not a completed one.

questions.prompt: The article then ___ how the policy changes society.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'shows' uses the historical present in a summary context.
Incorrect: 'showed' is simple past and would be less immediate.
Incorrect: 'has shown' is present perfect and less suitable for this narrative style.
Incorrect: 'is showing' suggests an ongoing process, not a summary point.

questions.prompt: They ___ the venue before the storm began.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'had inspected' is the past perfect, showing inspection completed before the storm.
Incorrect: 'inspected' is simple past and does not clearly show the sequence.
Incorrect: 'have inspected' is present perfect and does not anchor to past.
Incorrect: 'were inspecting' suggests the inspection was in progress, not completed.

questions.faultySentence: He discovered that the train already left.
questions.prompt: Correct the earlier past action using past perfect.
choices: He discovered that the train had already left.
He discovered that the train already left.
He discovered that the train has already left.
He discovered that the train left already.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'had already left' uses past perfect to show the train left before he discovered it.
Incorrect: This repeats the original error.
Incorrect: 'has already left' is present perfect and does not anchor to the past.
Incorrect: 'left already' is simple past and does not clearly show the sequence.

questions.faultySentence: The biography describes how the leader resigned and then escaped.
questions.prompt: Use a consistent historical present throughout.
choices: The biography describes how the leader resigns and then escapes.
The biography describes how the leader resigned and then escaped.
The biography described how the leader resigns and then escapes.
The biography describes how the leader resigned and then escapes.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Consistent use of historical present ('resigns', 'escapes') creates vivid narrative.
Incorrect: This mixes present and past tense inconsistently.
Incorrect: This mixes past and present tense inconsistently.
Incorrect: This has inconsistent tense use within the reported clause.

questions.prompt: By the time we arrived, the film ___ (start).
questions.explanation: 'had started' is the past perfect, marking the start as the earlier event in the past sequence.

questions.prompt: The story opens in Paris and then ___ (move) to Rome.
questions.explanation: 'moves' uses the historical present for a vivid plot summary.

questions.prompt: She was tired because she ___ (not sleep) well.
questions.explanation: 'had not slept' is the past perfect, explaining the cause before the past state.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence using past perfect.
questions.explanation: The past perfect event precedes the simple past reference point.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence using historical present.
questions.explanation: The historical present presents consecutive narrative events vividly.

topic.title: Advanced Future Meaning
topic.summary: Future forms express evidence-based prediction, intention, schedules, and arrangements from different viewpoints.

rules.title: Future prediction
rules.explanation: Will, be going to, and present forms express different kinds of prediction and evidence.
rules.example: Look at those clouds: it is going to rain.

rules.title: Future arrangements
rules.explanation: The present continuous presents a definite personal arrangement in the future.
rules.example: We are meeting the architect on Friday.

questions.prompt: The forecast says temperatures ___ overnight.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'will fall' is used for predictions based on external evidence (the forecast).
Incorrect: 'are falling' is present continuous and suggests a current action.
Incorrect: 'fall' is simple present and is not typically used for future predictions.
Incorrect: 'would fall' is conditional and does not fit the future prediction context.

questions.prompt: We ___ the board at ten tomorrow.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'are meeting' uses present continuous for a definite future arrangement.
Incorrect: 'meet' is simple present and typically used for scheduled events, not personal arrangements.
Incorrect: 'will meet' could work but lacks the 'arrangement' nuance.
Incorrect: 'have met' is present perfect and does not express future.

questions.prompt: Look out! You ___ that glass.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'are going to drop' is used for evidence-based predictions when the evidence is immediately visible.
Incorrect: 'will drop' could work but is less immediate than the evidence-based 'going to'.
Incorrect: 'drop' is simple present and is not used for future predictions.
Incorrect: 'would drop' is conditional and does not fit this context.

questions.prompt: She ___ her dentist next Tuesday.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'is seeing' uses present continuous for a definite future arrangement.
Incorrect: 'sees' is simple present and is less appropriate for personal arrangements.
Incorrect: 'will see' could work but lacks the 'arrangement' nuance.
Incorrect: 'has seen' is present perfect and does not express future.

questions.prompt: I think the plan ___ succeed.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'will' is used for predictions based on personal belief or opinion.
Incorrect: 'is going to' often suggests more immediate or evidenced predictions.
Incorrect: 'would' is conditional and suggests less certainty.
Incorrect: 'does' is simple present and does not express future.

questions.faultySentence: Look at the ice; it will fall through.
questions.prompt: Use an evidence-based prediction form.
choices: Look at the ice; it is going to fall through.
Look at the ice; it will fall through.
Look at the ice; it is falling through.
Look at the ice; it would fall through.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'is going to fall' uses the evidence-based prediction form, appropriate when the evidence is immediately visible.
Incorrect: This repeats the original error.
Incorrect: 'is falling' is present continuous and suggests it is happening now.
Incorrect: 'would fall' is conditional and does not fit the evidence-based prediction context.

questions.faultySentence: They will meeting the client at noon.
questions.prompt: Correct the arrangement expression.
choices: They are meeting the client at noon.
They will meet the client at noon.
They meet the client at noon.
They are meet the client at noon.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'are meeting' uses the present continuous for a definite future arrangement.
Incorrect: 'will meet' is grammatically possible but lacks the arrangement nuance.
Incorrect: 'meet' is simple present and is less appropriate for personal arrangements.
Incorrect: 'are meet' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: I am sure she ___ (pass) the exam.
questions.explanation: 'will pass' expresses a confident prediction based on personal belief.

questions.prompt: We ___ (fly) to Madrid next weekend.
questions.explanation: 'are flying' uses the present continuous to mark a planned arrangement.

questions.prompt: That ladder is unstable; it ___ (collapse).
questions.explanation: 'is going to collapse' is used when present evidence supports a prediction.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence expressing a future arrangement.
questions.explanation: The present continuous expresses the scheduled personal arrangement.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence expressing a prediction.
questions.explanation: 'Will' follows a prediction based on expressed judgement.

topic.title: Conditional Inversion
topic.summary: Formal conditional inversion removes 'if' and places 'were', 'had', or 'should' before the subject.

rules.title: Conditional inversion
rules.explanation: Formal conditionals can invert 'had', 'were', or 'should' before the subject without 'if'.
rules.example: Had I known, I would have called.

rules.title: Implied condition
rules.explanation: A condition can remain implicit when the surrounding context makes the hypothetical meaning clear.
rules.example: With more time, we could improve the design.

questions.prompt: ___ the risks been explained, we would have waited.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Had' inverts the third conditional clause 'If the risks had been explained'.
Incorrect: 'Have' would form an ungrammatical inversion here.
Incorrect: 'Were' is used for present hypotheticals, not past.
Incorrect: 'Should' is used for possible future conditions, not past.

questions.prompt: ___ you require assistance, contact reception.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Should' inverts the conditional 'If you should require assistance'.
Incorrect: 'Would' does not form a conditional inversion here.
Incorrect: 'Had' is for past conditions, not possible future.
Incorrect: 'Were' is for present hypotheticals, not future possibilities.

questions.prompt: With a larger budget, the team ___ expand the trial.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'could' expresses a hypothetical result of the implied condition.
Incorrect: 'will' suggests certainty rather than a hypothetical.
Incorrect: 'would have' is for past hypotheticals, not present.
Incorrect: 'can' suggests present ability, not hypothetical.

questions.prompt: ___ I in your position, I would reconsider.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Were' inverts the conditional 'If I were in your position'.
Incorrect: 'Was' is not used in formal subjunctive inversion.
Incorrect: 'Had' is used for past conditions, not present.
Incorrect: 'Should' is used for future possibilities, not present hypotheticals.

questions.prompt: The project might succeed, given ___ support.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'adequate' is the adjective modifying 'support' in the implied condition.
Incorrect: 'adequately' is an adverb and cannot modify the noun 'support'.
Incorrect: 'that adequate' is ungrammatical here.
Incorrect: 'the adequate' suggests definite rather than conditional support.

questions.faultySentence: Had I knew the deadline, I would have acted.
questions.prompt: Correct the inverted conditional form.
choices: Had I known the deadline, I would have acted.
Had I knew the deadline, I would have acted.
Had I know the deadline, I would have acted.
If I had known the deadline, I would have acted.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Had I known' uses the correct past participle form.
Incorrect: This repeats the error ('knew' instead of 'known').
Incorrect: 'Had I know' is ungrammatical.
Incorrect: This is grammatically correct but uses 'if' instead of inversion.

questions.faultySentence: With more staff, we will could finish sooner.
questions.prompt: Correct the implied condition expression.
choices: With more staff, we could finish sooner.
With more staff, we would finish sooner.
With more staff, we can finish sooner.
With more staff, we could to finish sooner.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'With more staff, we could finish' properly expresses the hypothetical result.
Incorrect: 'would' is less appropriate for a simple hypothetical result.
Incorrect: 'can' suggests actual ability, not hypothetical.
Incorrect: 'could to' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: ___ the weather improve, the event will continue.
questions.explanation: 'Should' inversion introduces a formal possible condition.

questions.prompt: Without your advice, I ___ have made a serious mistake.
questions.explanation: 'Might' expresses a hypothetical result of the implied condition.

questions.prompt: ___ she been informed, she would have objected.
questions.explanation: 'Had' plus the past participle inverts a third conditional.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence using conditional inversion.
questions.explanation: 'Had' inversion replaces 'If we had known' in formal writing.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence with an implied condition.
questions.explanation: The prepositional phrase implies the condition for the result.

topic.title: Advanced Mixed Conditionals
topic.summary: Mixed conditionals connect an unreal past cause with a present result, or a present state with a past result.

rules.title: Past condition, present result
rules.explanation: Use past perfect in the if-clause and 'would' plus a base verb for a present result.
rules.example: If I had taken the job, I would live abroad now.

rules.title: Present condition, past result
rules.explanation: Use past simple or 'were' in the if-clause and 'would have' plus a participle for a past result.
rules.example: If she were more careful, she would not have made that error.

questions.prompt: If he had accepted the offer, he ___ in London now.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'would live' is the present result of a past unreal condition.
Incorrect: 'would have lived' would be a past result, not a present one.
Incorrect: 'lived' is simple past and lacks the hypothetical meaning.
Incorrect: 'will live' expresses future certainty, not a hypothetical.

questions.prompt: If I were more organised, I ___ the deadline yesterday.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'would not have missed' is the past result of a present state.
Incorrect: 'would not miss' would be a present result.
Incorrect: 'did not miss' is simple past and lacks the hypothetical.
Incorrect: 'will not miss' expresses future, not past hypothetical.

questions.prompt: If they had invested earlier, they ___ richer today.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'would be' is the present result of a past condition.
Incorrect: 'would have been' would be a past result.
Incorrect: 'are' expresses present reality, not hypothetical.
Incorrect: 'will be' expresses future, not present hypothetical.

questions.prompt: If she knew the system, she ___ that mistake.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'would not have made' is the past result of a present state.
Incorrect: 'would not make' would be a present result.
Incorrect: 'did not make' is simple past and lacks the hypothetical.
Incorrect: 'will not make' expresses future, not past.

questions.prompt: If we had chosen the train, we ___ at home by now.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'would be' is the present result of a past condition.
Incorrect: 'would have been' would be a past result.
Incorrect: 'are' expresses present reality, not hypothetical.
Incorrect: 'were' is simple past and lacks the hypothetical meaning.

questions.faultySentence: If I had studied medicine, I would have work in a hospital now.
questions.prompt: Correct the present result form.
choices: If I had studied medicine, I would work in a hospital now.
If I had studied medicine, I would have worked in a hospital now.
If I studied medicine, I would work in a hospital now.
If I had studied medicine, I will work in a hospital now.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'would work' is the correct present result form.
Incorrect: 'would have worked' would be a past result, not present.
Incorrect: This changes the condition to a present unreal.
Incorrect: 'will work' expresses future, not present hypothetical.

questions.faultySentence: If he were more patient, he would not lose his temper yesterday.
questions.prompt: Correct the past result form.
choices: If he were more patient, he would not have lost his temper yesterday.
If he were more patient, he would not lose his temper yesterday.
If he was more patient, he would not have lost his temper yesterday.
If he were more patient, he will not have lost his temper yesterday.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'would not have lost' is the correct past result form.
Incorrect: This repeats the error ('would not lose' is present result).
Incorrect: 'was' is less formal than 'were' for hypotheticals.
Incorrect: 'will not have lost' expresses future, not past hypothetical.

questions.prompt: If she had moved abroad, she ___ (speak) another language now.
questions.explanation: 'would speak' is the present result of a past condition.

questions.prompt: If I were braver, I ___ (apply) for that role last year.
questions.explanation: 'would have applied' is the past result of a present hypothetical state.

questions.prompt: If we had saved more, we ___ (not worry) about money now.
questions.explanation: 'would not be worrying' uses the continuous present result form.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct mixed conditional sentence.
questions.explanation: The past perfect condition has a present 'would' result.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct mixed conditional sentence.
questions.explanation: The present state has a past perfect result.

topic.title: Subjunctive and Mandative Forms
topic.summary: Formal recommendations and demands use the mandative subjunctive and established formulaic expressions.

rules.title: Mandative subjunctive
rules.explanation: After verbs and adjectives of demand or importance, formal English can use the base form for all subjects.
rules.example: The committee recommended that he attend.

rules.title: Formulaic subjunctive
rules.explanation: Fixed phrases preserve subjunctive forms such as 'be' in wishes, demands, and formal expressions.
rules.example: Long live the republic.

questions.prompt: They insisted that she ___ present.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'be' is the mandative subjunctive form used after 'insisted'.
Incorrect: 'is' is indicative, not subjunctive.
Incorrect: 'was' is past tense, not mandative subjunctive.
Incorrect: 'being' is a participle, not the subjunctive base form.

questions.prompt: It is vital that every member ___ informed.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'be' is the mandative subjunctive form used after 'It is vital that'.
Incorrect: 'is' is indicative, not subjunctive.
Incorrect: 'was' is past tense, not mandative subjunctive.
Incorrect: 'being' is a participle, not the subjunctive base form.

questions.prompt: ___ it be noted that the figures are provisional.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Let' is used in the formulaic subjunctive expression 'Let it be noted'.
Incorrect: 'Lets' is not used in this formulaic expression.
Incorrect: 'May' would suggest permission rather than a formal directive.
Incorrect: 'Shall' is not used in this formulaic expression.

questions.prompt: The doctor recommended that he ___ smoking.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'stop' is the mandative subjunctive form used after 'recommended'.
Incorrect: 'stops' is indicative, not subjunctive.
Incorrect: 'stopped' is past tense, not mandative subjunctive.
Incorrect: 'stopping' is a participle, not the base form.

questions.prompt: The formal phrase is "___ peace prevail."
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'May' is used in the formulaic subjunctive expression 'May peace prevail'.
Incorrect: 'Mays' is ungrammatical.
Incorrect: 'Let' would be 'Let peace prevail', which is possible but not the exact expression.
Incorrect: 'Shall' is not used in this formulaic expression.

questions.faultySentence: The panel demanded that the report is revised.
questions.prompt: Use the formal mandative subjunctive form.
choices: The panel demanded that the report be revised.
The panel demanded that the report is revised.
The panel demanded that the report was revised.
The panel demanded that the report to be revised.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'be revised' is the mandative subjunctive form.
Incorrect: This repeats the original error.
Incorrect: 'was revised' is past tense, not mandative subjunctive.
Incorrect: 'to be revised' is an infinitive, not the subjunctive.

questions.faultySentence: Long lives the king.
questions.prompt: Correct the formulaic subjunctive expression.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Long live the king' is the fixed subjunctive expression.
Incorrect: This repeats the original error.
Incorrect: This changes the expression significantly.
Incorrect: This is ungrammatical in this context.

questions.prompt: It is essential that she ___ (remain) calm.
questions.explanation: The base form 'remain' follows an adjective of importance in formal English.

questions.prompt: They proposed that the rule ___ (change).
questions.explanation: The passive mandative subjunctive uses 'be' plus a past participle.

questions.prompt: Heaven ___ (help) us.
questions.explanation: This fixed expression uses the base form after the subject.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence using the mandative subjunctive.
questions.explanation: 'Insist' can introduce a formal mandative subjunctive clause.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence using a formulaic subjunctive.
questions.explanation: 'May' introduces a formal wish or blessing.

topic.title: Advanced Passive and Get-Passive
topic.summary: Passive choices foreground events and participants, while 'get'-passives often highlight change or involvement.

rules.title: Get-passive constructions
rules.explanation: 'Get'-passives often describe a change of state or an event affecting the subject in less formal styles.
rules.example: He got promoted last year.

rules.title: Passive reporting structures
rules.explanation: 'It is believed' and 'he is believed to' report information while keeping the source impersonal.
rules.example: She is believed to have left.

questions.prompt: The old bridge ___ damaged in the storm.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'got' in the get-passive construction emphasises the change of state.
Incorrect: 'was' is the standard passive but lacks the change-of-state emphasis.
Incorrect: 'had been' is past perfect passive, not the get-passive.
Incorrect: 'has' is not a passive form.

questions.prompt: The witness is believed ___ abroad.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to be living' is the continuous infinitive used in passive reporting.
Incorrect: 'to live' is possible but lacks the continuous aspect.
Incorrect: 'living' cannot follow 'is believed'.
Incorrect: 'that lives' does not follow the passive reporting structure.

questions.prompt: Try not to ___ caught in the traffic.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'get' in the get-passive construction emphasises the state change.
Incorrect: 'be' is the standard passive but less idiomatic here.
Incorrect: 'become' is not used in this passive construction.
Incorrect: 'have' cannot form a passive here.

questions.prompt: The results are expected ___ tomorrow.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to be published' is the passive infinitive in the reporting structure.
Incorrect: 'to publish' would be the active infinitive.
Incorrect: 'publishing' cannot follow 'are expected'.
Incorrect: 'that they publish' does not follow the expected structure.

questions.prompt: She ___ promoted after leading the team.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'got' in the get-passive construction emphasises the change of state.
Incorrect: 'was' is the standard passive but lacks the emphasis.
Incorrect: 'has' is not a passive form.
Incorrect: 'had' is not a passive form here.

questions.faultySentence: He got fire for missing the deadline.
questions.prompt: Correct the get-passive form.
choices: He got fired for missing the deadline.
He was fired for missing the deadline.
He got firing for missing the deadline.
He got to fire for missing the deadline.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'got fired' is the correct get-passive form.
Incorrect: 'was fired' is standard passive but not the get-passive.
Incorrect: 'got firing' is not a passive form.
Incorrect: 'got to fire' is ungrammatical.

questions.faultySentence: She is believed to left the country.
questions.prompt: Correct the passive reporting structure.
choices: She is believed to have left the country.
She is believed to leave the country.
She is believed left the country.
She believed to have left the country.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to have left' is the perfect infinitive used in passive reporting.
Incorrect: 'to leave' would be present infinitive, suggesting future.
Incorrect: 'left' cannot follow 'is believed to'.
Incorrect: 'believed' without 'is' is not passive.

questions.prompt: The players ___ (get / exhaust) during the final.
questions.explanation: 'got exhausted' uses 'get' plus the past participle to present a change of state.

questions.prompt: The company is thought ___ (develop) a new process.
questions.explanation: 'to be developing' reports an action believed to be in progress.

questions.prompt: The artefact is known ___ (date) from the sixth century.
questions.explanation: The simple infinitive follows a present reporting claim.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct get-passive sentence.
questions.explanation: The get-passive highlights the event affecting the subject.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct passive reporting sentence.
questions.explanation: The perfect infinitive places the escape before the reporting viewpoint.

topic.title: Passive with Two Objects
topic.summary: Verbs with two objects allow alternative passive structures, including personal and prepositional passives.

rules.title: Double-object passives
rules.explanation: With verbs such as 'give' and 'send', either object can become the passive subject when the result is clear.
rules.example: She was given a second chance.

rules.title: Prepositional passives
rules.explanation: The object of a preposition can become the subject while the preposition remains at the end.
rules.example: This is the topic I was referring to.

questions.prompt: The students ___ extra time.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'were given' is the double-object passive with the recipient as subject.
Incorrect: 'gave' is active voice.
Incorrect: 'were giving' is active continuous.
Incorrect: 'had given' is active past perfect.

questions.prompt: The issue was ___ by the committee.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'dealt with' keeps the preposition in the passive.
Incorrect: 'dealt' is not transitive in this sense without 'with'.
Incorrect: 'dealing with' is active.
Incorrect: 'dealt to' changes the meaning.

questions.prompt: A detailed explanation ___ to the visitors.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'was given' is the double-object passive with the object as subject.
Incorrect: 'gave' is active.
Incorrect: 'was giving' is active continuous.
Incorrect: 'had given' is active.

questions.prompt: That is the principle on which the system ___.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'is based' is the passive form with the preposition 'on'.
Incorrect: 'bases' is active.
Incorrect: 'is basing' is active.
Incorrect: 'had based' is active past perfect.

questions.prompt: The client ___ a full refund.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'was sent' is the double-object passive with the recipient as subject.
Incorrect: 'sent' is active.
Incorrect: 'was sending' is active.
Incorrect: 'had sent' is active.

questions.faultySentence: The assistant was explained the procedure.
questions.prompt: Correct the double-object passive form.
choices: The procedure was explained to the assistant.
The assistant was explained the procedure.
The procedure was explained the assistant.
The assistant was explained to the procedure.
choiceExplanations: Correct: With 'explain', the thing is the passive subject.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Incorrect: Missing the necessary preposition 'to'.
Incorrect: Incorrect use of the preposition.

questions.faultySentence: This is the problem which we are dealing.
questions.prompt: Correct the prepositional passive by keeping the preposition.
choices: This is the problem which we are dealing with.
This is the problem which we are dealing.
This is the problem with which we are dealing.
This is the problem we are dealing.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'dealing with' retains the necessary preposition.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Incorrect: This is grammatically correct but overly formal.
Incorrect: Missing the preposition.

questions.prompt: The winner ___ (offer) a scholarship.
questions.explanation: The recipient becomes the subject of the passive 'offer'.

questions.prompt: The proposal was strongly ___ (object) by residents.
questions.explanation: 'Object to' keeps its preposition in the passive.

questions.prompt: A copy of the report ___ (send) to every member.
questions.explanation: The thing transferred becomes the passive subject.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct double-object passive sentence.
questions.explanation: The indirect object becomes the passive subject with 'offer'.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct prepositional passive sentence.
questions.explanation: The preposition stays with the passive verb.

topic.title: Advanced Reported Discourse
topic.summary: Reported discourse balances optional backshift with the speaker's current viewpoint and preserves modal meaning.

rules.title: Optional backshift
rules.explanation: Backshift is often optional when a reported fact remains current or generally true.
rules.example: The lecturer said that water boils at 100°C.

rules.title: Reported modality
rules.explanation: Reported speech preserves the strength and time reference of modal meanings.
rules.example: She said she might return later.

questions.prompt: The guide said that the museum ___ at nine.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'opens' retains present tense as the fact remains current.
Incorrect: 'opened' is backshifted but unnecessary for a repeated fact.
Incorrect: 'has opened' suggests a completed action, not a regular schedule.
Incorrect: 'is opening' suggests an ongoing action.

questions.prompt: He said he ___ be late.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'might' correctly backshifts 'may' in reported speech.
Incorrect: 'may' could be used but 'might' is the standard backshift.
Incorrect: 'would' changes the meaning from possibility to intention.
Incorrect: 'could' changes the meaning to ability.

questions.prompt: She explained that the machine ___ correctly.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'was working' is the natural backshift for a past report.
Incorrect: 'is working' may be acceptable if still true.
Incorrect: 'worked' suggests a completed action, not a state.
Incorrect: 'has worked' suggests completed actions, not a current state.

questions.prompt: They warned us that the road ___ be closed.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'could' backshifts 'can' in the warning.
Incorrect: 'can' might be used but 'could' is the standard backshift.
Incorrect: 'will' changes the meaning to certainty.
Incorrect: 'may' could be used but 'could' is more appropriate after 'warned'.

questions.prompt: The professor said that light ___ faster than sound.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'travels' retains present tense as a universal fact.
Incorrect: 'travelled' is backshifted but unnecessary for a universal truth.
Incorrect: 'has travelled' suggests a completed action.
Incorrect: 'is travelling' suggests an ongoing action.

questions.faultySentence: The scientist said that water boiled at 100°C and it still does.
questions.prompt: Use an appropriate present fact form.
choices: The scientist said that water boils at 100°C and it still does.
The scientist said that water boiled at 100°C and it still does.
The scientist said that water has boiled at 100°C and it still does.
The scientist said that water is boiling at 100°C and it still does.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'boils' uses the present for a universal fact.
Incorrect: This repeats the unnecessary backshift.
Incorrect: 'has boiled' is a completed action, not a general fact.
Incorrect: 'is boiling' suggests an ongoing action.

questions.faultySentence: She said she might to return later.
questions.prompt: Correct the reported modal form.
choices: She said she might return later.
She said she might return later.
She said she might returned later.
She said she may return later.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'might return' uses the modal without 'to'.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Incorrect: 'might returned' is ungrammatical.
Incorrect: 'may return' might be used but 'might' is the standard backshift.

questions.prompt: He said that he ___ (need) more time.
questions.explanation: 'needed' backshifts a past report of a current need.

questions.prompt: She said that she ___ (may) join us later.
questions.explanation: 'May' commonly backshifts to 'might' in reported speech.

questions.prompt: The manual states that the device ___ (require) two batteries.
questions.explanation: 'Requires' retains the present tense for a current instruction.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct reported speech sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Might' reports a possible change without adding 'to'.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct reported speech sentence.
questions.explanation: The present is retained because the rule remains current.

topic.title: Quotative and Reporting Style
topic.summary: Reporting verbs and quotative patterns organise direct speech while making the source and stance clear.

rules.title: Quotative inversion
rules.explanation: Narrative reporting can place the reporting verb before the subject, especially after a quotation.
rules.example: "I agree," replied Maya.

rules.title: Reporting the source
rules.explanation: Reporting structures identify whether information comes from a person, document, or less certain source.
rules.example: According to the report, the figures have changed.

questions.prompt: "That is impossible," ___ the witness.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'replied' is an appropriate reporting verb for a response.
Incorrect: 'said' is also possible but 'replied' better fits the context.
Incorrect: 'stated' is more formal and less conversational.
Incorrect: 'told' requires an object and doesn't fit this inversion pattern.

questions.prompt: ___ the latest figures, demand has increased.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'According to' is the standard phrase for citing a source.
Incorrect: 'According with' is not standard.
Incorrect: 'Based on' could be used but 'According to' is more common.
Incorrect: 'Following' would suggest chronological order, not source.

questions.prompt: "Leave now," ___ the officer.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'ordered' appropriately reports a command.
Incorrect: 'said' is neutral and lacks the command sense.
Incorrect: 'told' requires an object and doesn't invert naturally.
Incorrect: 'commanded' is possible but 'ordered' is more direct.

questions.prompt: The report ___ that the policy had failed.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'suggests' is a neutral reporting verb for a document.
Incorrect: 'indicates' is also possible but 'suggests' is more common.
Incorrect: 'states' is more direct than the prompt's context.
Incorrect: 'argues' suggests a position, not a neutral report.

questions.prompt: "I have finished," ___ Noor.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'said' is a standard neutral reporting verb.
Incorrect: 'replied' would only work if responding to someone.
Incorrect: 'stated' is more formal than necessary.
Incorrect: 'announced' suggests a public declaration.

questions.faultySentence: "I am ready," said did the candidate.
questions.prompt: Correct the quotative inversion structure.
choices: "I am ready," said did the candidate.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'said the candidate' uses standard quotative inversion.
Incorrect: This repeats the error with 'did'.
Incorrect: This is possible but not inversion.
Correct: This is also a possible correct answer.

questions.faultySentence: According the report, the figures are stable.
questions.prompt: Complete the source phrase correctly.
choices: According to the report, the figures are stable.
According the report, the figures are stable.
Based on the report, the figures are stable.
Following the report, the figures are stable.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'According to' is the correct phrase.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Incorrect: 'Based on' could work but is not the literal correction.
Incorrect: 'Following' suggests chronological order, not source.

questions.prompt: "We object," ___ (say) the residents.
questions.explanation: 'Said' can follow a quotation before the reporting subject.

questions.prompt: The survey ___ (indicate) a change in public opinion.
questions.explanation: 'Indicates' presents what the survey communicates.

questions.prompt: ___ (base) on the evidence, the claim is plausible.
questions.explanation: 'Based on' introduces the evidence supporting a conclusion.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct quotative inversion sentence.
questions.explanation: The reporting verb is inverted after the direct quotation.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence citing a source.
questions.explanation: 'According to' identifies the documentary source.

topic.title: Relative Clauses and Information Structure
topic.summary: Relative clauses attach modifiers clearly and distinguish restrictive from supplementary information.

rules.title: Relative clause attachment
rules.explanation: Place a relative clause next to the noun it modifies and use a suitable relative form.
rules.example: The report that the committee released clarified the policy.

rules.title: Resumptive reference
rules.explanation: Formal English normally omits a repeated object after a relative pronoun.
rules.example: The proposal that we discussed was approved.

questions.prompt: The engineer ___ designed the bridge won the award.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'who' is the relative pronoun for a person in subject position.
Incorrect: 'that' is possible but 'who' is preferred for a person.
Incorrect: 'which' is for things, not people.
Incorrect: 'whom' is for objects, not subjects.

questions.prompt: The book that I recommended ___ useful.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'was' completes the sentence without a resumptive pronoun.
Incorrect: 'it was' uses an unnecessary resumptive pronoun.
Incorrect: 'being' is not a finite verb.
Incorrect: 'had been' suggests past completed action, not a present evaluation.

questions.prompt: The office, ___ overlooks the harbour, is being renovated.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'which' is used for non-defining relative clauses.
Incorrect: 'that' is not typically used in non-defining clauses.
Incorrect: 'what' is not a relative pronoun.
Incorrect: 'whose' is possessive and doesn't fit here.

questions.prompt: The issue ___ we discussed remains unresolved.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'that' introduces the object relative clause without a resumptive pronoun.
Incorrect: 'which' is also possible but 'that' is more common.
Incorrect: 'what' is not a relative pronoun.
Incorrect: 'where' would be for a place.

questions.faultySentence: The analyst spoke to the manager who was waiting in the lobby.
questions.prompt: Make the attachment clear if the analyst was waiting, not the manager.
choices: The analyst who was waiting in the lobby spoke to the manager.
The analyst spoke to the manager who was waiting in the lobby.
The analyst, who was waiting in the lobby, spoke to the manager.
The analyst who was waiting in the lobby spoke to the manager.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Placing 'who' after 'analyst' shows the analyst was waiting.
Incorrect: This attaches 'who' to 'manager'.
Correct: This also makes it clear the analyst was waiting.
Correct: This is a valid alternative.

questions.faultySentence: The plan which we approved it starts tomorrow.
questions.prompt: Remove the resumptive pronoun error.
choices: The plan which we approved starts tomorrow.
The plan which we approved it starts tomorrow.
The plan we approved starts tomorrow.
The plan which we approved starts tomorrow.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Removes the unnecessary resumptive pronoun 'it'.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Correct: This is also grammatically correct.
Correct: This is a valid alternative.

questions.faultySentence: The laboratory, that opened last year, is expanding.
questions.prompt: Correct the non-defining relative clause.
choices: The laboratory, which opened last year, is expanding.
The laboratory that opened last year is expanding.
The laboratory, which opened last year, is expanding.
The laboratory which opened last year is expanding.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Non-defining relative clauses use 'which', not 'that'.
Correct: If restrictive, 'that' is possible but with no commas.
Correct: This is the standard non-defining form.
Correct: This is acceptable without commas.

questions.prompt: The researcher ___ (who / whom) led the study presented the findings.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the subject of 'led' in the relative clause.

questions.prompt: The evidence ___ we found was conclusive.
questions.explanation: 'That' introduces the object relative clause without a repeated pronoun.

questions.prompt: The village in ___ she grew up has changed.
questions.explanation: 'Which' follows the preposition 'in' in a formal relative clause.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct restrictive relative clause sentence.
questions.explanation: The defining clause follows the noun it identifies.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct relative clause sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Whom' represents the object and is not followed by a resumptive pronoun.

topic.title: Nominal Relative Clauses
topic.summary: Nominal relatives function as noun phrases and express things, people, or choices without an antecedent.

rules.title: Nominal relative 'what'
rules.explanation: 'What' means 'the thing or things that' and introduces a clause functioning as a noun phrase.
rules.example: What she said surprised everyone.

rules.title: Nominal relative 'whoever'
rules.explanation: 'Whoever' and 'whatever' refer generally to any person or thing meeting the condition.
rules.example: Whoever arrives first can choose a seat.

questions.prompt: ___ he proposed was financially realistic.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'What' means 'the thing that' and functions as the subject.
Incorrect: 'Which' would need an antecedent.
Incorrect: 'That' would need a noun to modify.
Incorrect: 'Whatever' suggests any proposal, not a specific one.

questions.prompt: ___ answers correctly may leave early.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Whoever' functions as the subject of the entire sentence.
Incorrect: 'Who' would be a relative pronoun requiring an antecedent.
Incorrect: 'Anyone who' is possible but not a nominal relative.
Incorrect: 'Whomever' would be for an object position.

questions.prompt: Take ___ you need from the cupboard.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Whatever' means 'anything that' and fits the general permission.
Incorrect: 'What' is too specific.
Incorrect: 'Which' would require a specific choice.
Incorrect: 'That' would require an antecedent.

questions.prompt: We will support ___ the panel selects.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Whoever' is used as the object of 'selects'.
Incorrect: 'Whomever' is technically correct as an object, but less common.
Incorrect: 'Who' would need an antecedent.
Incorrect: 'Whom' would need an antecedent.

questions.faultySentence: What that she explained was helpful.
questions.prompt: Use one nominal relative marker correctly.
choices: That which she explained was helpful.
The thing that she explained was helpful.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'What' is the only nominal relative needed.
Correct: This is also a valid, albeit formal, alternative.
Correct: This is the standard form.
Correct: This is a possible expansion.

questions.faultySentence: Whoever he will apply may request an interview.
questions.prompt: Correct the nominal relative clause.
choices: Whoever applies may request an interview.
Whoever will apply may request an interview.
Whoever apply may request an interview.
Anyone who applies may request an interview.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Whoever applies' is the standard nominal relative form.
Incorrect: 'will apply' is unnecessary with 'whoever'.
Incorrect: 'apply' is plural and doesn't agree with singular 'whoever'.
Correct: This is a possible alternative.

questions.faultySentence: I cannot accept which you have suggested.
questions.prompt: Replace the incorrect relative form.
choices: I cannot accept what you have suggested.
I cannot accept that which you have suggested.
I cannot accept whatever you have suggested.
I cannot accept what you have suggested.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'What' means 'the thing that'.
Correct: This is a valid formal alternative.
Correct: This is also valid if 'anything' is meant.
Correct: This is the standard form.

questions.prompt: ___ matters most is reliability.
questions.explanation: 'What' functions as the noun phrase meaning 'the thing that matters'.

questions.prompt: ___ you invite will need a pass.
questions.explanation: 'Whoever' refers to any person you invite.

questions.prompt: Choose ___ seems most practical.
questions.explanation: 'Whatever' means 'anything that seems most practical'.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct nominal relative sentence.
questions.explanation: The nominal relative clause is the subject of 'was'.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct nominal relative sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Whoever' introduces the subject of the main clause.

topic.title: Advanced Complementation
topic.summary: Complement patterns control whether clauses take infinitives, -ing forms, or that-clauses after complex verbs.

rules.title: Complex complementation
rules.explanation: Different verbs select different complement patterns, including that-clauses, infinitives, and gerunds.
rules.example: The committee recommended that the plan be revised.

rules.title: Raising verbs
rules.explanation: Raising verbs allow the apparent subject of an infinitive to relate to the main clause without assigning it a main-clause role.
rules.example: The results appear to confirm the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: They insisted ___ the contract immediately.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'on signing' uses the preposition 'on' with the gerund.
Incorrect: 'to sign' is an infinitive and doesn't follow 'insist'.
Incorrect: 'that signing' is ungrammatical.
Incorrect: 'sign' is the base form without the necessary structure.

questions.prompt: The results appear ___ the original prediction.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to support' is the infinitive complement of the raising verb 'appear'.
Incorrect: 'to be supporting' is possible but less direct.
Incorrect: 'supporting' is a gerund, not used after 'appear'.
Incorrect: 'that support' is a finite clause, not used after 'appear'.

questions.prompt: She suggested ___ the meeting.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'postponing' is the gerund complement of 'suggested'.
Incorrect: 'to postpone' is an infinitive, not used after 'suggest'.
Incorrect: 'that postpone' is ungrammatical.
Incorrect: 'postpone' is the base form without the necessary structure.

questions.prompt: The device is believed ___ safe.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to be' is the infinitive complement of the raising verb in passive.
Incorrect: 'being' is a gerund, not used in this pattern.
Incorrect: 'that it is' is a finite clause, not used after passive 'believe'.
Incorrect: 'be' is the base form without 'to'.

questions.faultySentence: The adviser recommended us to revise the proposal.
questions.prompt: Use the appropriate complement pattern for 'recommend'.
choices: The adviser recommended that we revise the proposal.
The adviser recommended us revising the proposal.
The adviser recommended to us to revise the proposal.
The adviser recommended we revise the proposal.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'recommended that we revise' uses the that-clause pattern.
Incorrect: 'recommended us revising' is not a standard pattern.
Incorrect: 'recommended to us' is awkward.
Correct: 'recommended we revise' is also acceptable (subjunctive).

questions.faultySentence: The figures appear that they contradict the forecast.
questions.prompt: Correct the raising construction.
choices: The figures appear to contradict the forecast.
The figures appear that they contradict the forecast.
It appears that the figures contradict the forecast.
The figures appear to be contradicting the forecast.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'appear to contradict' is the standard raising construction.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Correct: This is a valid alternative using extraposition.
Correct: This is a possible continuous infinitive alternative.

questions.faultySentence: He avoided to answer the question.
questions.prompt: Correct the complement after 'avoid'.
choices: He avoided to answer the question.
He avoided that he answered the question.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'avoided answering' uses the gerund pattern.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Incorrect: 'avoided that' is not a standard pattern.
Incorrect: 'avoided answer' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: The board agreed ___ (extend) the deadline.
questions.explanation: 'Agree' takes a to-infinitive when the subject undertakes an action.

questions.prompt: The proposal seems ___ (address) the main concern.
questions.explanation: 'Seem' takes a to-infinitive complement.

questions.prompt: They objected to ___ (change) the schedule.
questions.explanation: The preposition 'to' is followed by an -ing form here.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct raising verb sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Seem' is followed by a to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct complement pattern sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Recommend' can take an -ing complement.

topic.title: Control and Infinitive Subjects
topic.summary: Control constructions distinguish the understood subject of an infinitive from an explicit 'for'-to subject.

rules.title: Control infinitives
rules.explanation: In control constructions, a noun phrase in the main clause supplies the understood subject of the infinitive.
rules.example: The students agreed to revise the draft.

rules.title: 'For'-to subjects
rules.explanation: Use 'for' plus a noun phrase before an infinitive when its subject differs from the main-clause subject.
rules.example: It is important for every applicant to register.

questions.prompt: The manager persuaded the team ___ earlier.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to leave' is the to-infinitive controlled by 'the team'.
Incorrect: 'leaving' is a gerund, not used after 'persuaded'.
Incorrect: 'that leave' is ungrammatical.
Incorrect: 'leave' is the base form without 'to'.

questions.prompt: It is unusual ___ the machine to fail.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'for' introduces the explicit subject of the infinitive.
Incorrect: 'of it' is not used in this pattern.
Incorrect: 'that' would introduce a finite clause.
Incorrect: 'about' is not used in this pattern.

questions.prompt: The witness refused ___ the statement.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to sign' is the to-infinitive controlled by the witness.
Incorrect: 'signing' is a gerund, not used after 'refused'.
Incorrect: 'that sign' is ungrammatical.
Incorrect: 'sign' is the base form without 'to'.

questions.prompt: There is no reason ___ us to delay.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'for' introduces the explicit subject of the infinitive.
Incorrect: 'that' would introduce a finite clause.
Incorrect: 'about' is not used in this pattern.
Incorrect: 'of' is not used in this pattern.

questions.faultySentence: The coach encouraged to the players practise daily.
questions.prompt: Correct the object-control construction.
choices: The coach encouraged the players to practise daily.
The coach encouraged the players practise daily.
The coach encouraged to the players to practise daily.
The coach encouraged that the players practise daily.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'encouraged the players to practise' is the correct object-control form.
Incorrect: 'encouraged the players practise' lacks the infinitive marker.
Incorrect: 'encouraged to the players' is ungrammatical.
Correct: This is also a valid alternative.

questions.faultySentence: It was difficult the interns to understand the procedure.
questions.prompt: Add the explicit infinitive subject marker.
choices: It was difficult for the interns to understand the procedure.
It was difficult to the interns to understand the procedure.
It was difficult that the interns understood the procedure.
It was difficult for the interns understand the procedure.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'for the interns' introduces the explicit subject.
Incorrect: 'to the interns' is not used in this pattern.
Incorrect: 'that' introduces a finite clause, not an infinitive.
Incorrect: Missing the infinitive marker 'to' after 'understand'.

questions.faultySentence: The child promised her mother to behave.
questions.prompt: Make the controlled subject clear.
choices: The child promised her mother that she would behave.
The child promised to her mother to behave.
The child promised her mother she would behave.
The child promised her mother to behave.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'that she would behave' clarifies who will behave.
Incorrect: 'promised to her mother' is less clear.
Correct: This is also possible with the subjunctive.
Incorrect: This repeats the original ambiguity.

questions.prompt: The committee allowed the visitors ___ (enter).
questions.explanation: 'Allow' takes an object plus a to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: It is essential ___ applicants to provide identification.
questions.explanation: 'For' introduces 'applicants' as the subject of 'to provide'.

questions.prompt: She managed ___ (solve) the puzzle.
questions.explanation: 'Manage' takes a to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct 'for-to' subject sentence.
questions.explanation: 'For' marks the subject of the infinitive.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct control infinitive sentence.
questions.explanation: The object 'us' controls the understood subject of 'ask'.

topic.title: Modality and Evidentiality
topic.summary: Modal choices grade certainty while evidential expressions show how a claim is supported.

rules.title: Epistemic modality scale
rules.explanation: Epistemic modals express different degrees of certainty about a proposition.
rules.example: The delay may be caused by a technical fault.

rules.title: Evidential language
rules.explanation: Evidential phrases identify whether a claim comes from observation, report, or inference.
rules.example: The evidence suggests that demand is falling.

questions.prompt: The lights are on, so someone ___ be inside.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'must' expresses a strong logical inference based on evidence.
Incorrect: 'may' suggests possibility, not the strong inference implied.
Incorrect: 'could' is less certain than 'must'.
Incorrect: 'might' is the least certain of the options.

questions.prompt: The data ___ indicate a seasonal pattern.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'appear to' is an evidential expression suggesting inference.
Incorrect: 'appear that' would need a finite clause.
Incorrect: 'seem that' would also need a finite clause.
Incorrect: 'indicate that' is more direct than evidential.

questions.prompt: The parcel ___ have arrived; the doorbell rang.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'may' expresses possibility consistent with the evidence.
Incorrect: 'must' would be too certain for this context.
Incorrect: 'can' is not used in this epistemic sense.
Incorrect: 'will' expresses future certainty, not past inference.

questions.prompt: According to witnesses, the vehicle ___ left at noon.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'appears to have' is the evidential expression with perfect infinitive.
Incorrect: 'appears that' would need a finite clause.
Correct: 'seems to have' is also possible.
Incorrect: 'is appearing' is not used in this evidential sense.

questions.faultySentence: The explanation must to be wrong.
questions.prompt: Correct the epistemic modal form.
choices: The explanation must to be wrong.
The explanation must have been wrong.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'must be' is the correct epistemic modal form.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Incorrect: This changes the meaning to past inference.
Incorrect: 'wrongly' is an adverb, not an adjective.

questions.faultySentence: The results suggest us that the treatment works.
questions.prompt: Use an appropriate evidential pattern.
choices: The results suggest that the treatment works.
The results suggest the treatment works.
The results suggest us that the treatment works.
The results suggest to us that the treatment works.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'suggest that' is the standard evidential pattern.
Correct: This is also possible without 'that'.
Incorrect: This repeats the error with 'us'.
Incorrect: This is awkward; 'suggest to' is not standard.

questions.faultySentence: She may has misunderstood the instruction.
questions.prompt: Correct the modal perfect form.
choices: She may have misunderstood the instruction.
She may has misunderstood the instruction.
She might have misunderstood the instruction.
She may have misunderstand the instruction.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'may have misunderstood' is the correct modal perfect form.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Correct: 'might have' is also a possible alternative.
Incorrect: 'misunderstand' is the base form, not past participle.

questions.prompt: The keys are missing, so he ___ (must / lose) them.
questions.explanation: 'Must have lost' expresses a strong inference about the past.

questions.prompt: The witness report ___ (indicate) that the door was open.
questions.explanation: 'Indicates' is the evidential verb with the report as the grammatical subject.

questions.prompt: They ___ (might / overlook) a crucial detail.
questions.explanation: 'Might have overlooked' expresses a tentative past inference.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct evidential sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Appear to' presents an inference based on evidence.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct epistemic modal sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Must have been' marks a strong past inference.

topic.title: Politeness and Interpersonal Modality
topic.summary: Tentative forms and negative-politeness strategies soften requests, disagreement, and imposition.

rules.title: Tentative language

topic.title: Focus and Prosody in Writing
topic.summary: Fronting and focus particles highlight contrast or priority while preserving the intended information structure.

topic.title: Clefts and Pseudo-clefts

topic.title: Advanced Inversion
topic.summary: Inversion after restrictive adverbials and locative phrases creates formal emphasis and marked information order.

rules.title: Gapping
rules.explanation: Gapping omits a repeated verb and auxiliary in a non-initial coordinated clause.
rules.example: Mina chose the venue, and Theo the date.

rules.title: Comparative ellipsis
rules.explanation: Comparatives can omit repeated material when the comparison remains clear.
rules.example: The second test was more reliable than the first.

questions.prompt: I approved the design, and Sam ___ the budget.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'the' is the remaining object in the gapped clause.
Incorrect: 'approved the' repeats the verb unnecessarily.
Incorrect: 'did the' is not the correct gapping form.
Incorrect: 'was the' changes the meaning.

questions.prompt: The revised model is faster than the original ___.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'one' stands in for the repeated noun 'model'.
Incorrect: 'is' would be unnecessary repetition.
Incorrect: 'does' is not used in this comparative.
Incorrect: 'model' repeats the noun unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Nora selected the topic, and Lee ___ the method.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'the' is the remaining object in the gapped clause.
Incorrect: 'selected the' repeats the verb unnecessarily.
Incorrect: 'did the' is not the correct gapping form.
Incorrect: 'was the' changes the meaning.

questions.prompt: This explanation is clearer than the previous ___.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'one' stands in for the repeated noun 'explanation'.
Incorrect: 'was' would be unnecessary repetition.
Incorrect: 'does' is not used in this comparative.
Incorrect: 'explanation' repeats the noun unnecessarily.

questions.faultySentence: The first group chose the room, and the second group chose the time.

choices: The first group chose the room, and the second group the time.
The first group chose the room, and the second chose the time.
The first group chose the room, and the second the time.
The first group chose the room, and the second group time.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Gapping removes the repeated verb.
Correct: This is also correct, removing the second 'chose'.
Correct: This is the most concise gapping form.

choices: The new version is more efficient than the old one.
The new version is more efficient than the old version.
The new version is more efficient than the old.
The new version is more efficient than is the old one.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'the old one' is the standard comparative ellipsis.
Correct: This is also correct but repeats 'version'.
Correct: This is also acceptable with the adjective.
Incorrect: This repeats the original inversion.

questions.faultySentence: I prepared the slides, and Priya prepared the handout.
questions.prompt: Make the second clause elliptical.
choices: I prepared the slides, and Priya the handout.
I prepared the slides, and Priya prepared the handout.
I prepared the slides, and the handout by Priya.
I prepared the slides, and Priya the handout.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Gapping removes the repeated verb.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Incorrect: This changes the structure awkwardly.
Correct: This is the correct gapped form.

questions.explanation: Gapping leaves the second subject and object after coordination.

questions.explanation: 'One' stands for the repeated singular noun 'draft'.
