questions.explanation: 'One' replaces the repeated noun 'route'.

topic.title: Concession and Scalar Meaning
topic.summary: Concessive clauses mark unexpected contrasts, while scalar expressions strengthen or widen the contrast.

rules.title: Concessive clauses
rules.explanation: 'Although' and 'even though' introduce a condition that contrasts with the main result.
rules.example: Although the route was long, it was efficient.

rules.title: Scalar 'even if'
rules.explanation: 'Even if' presents a hypothetical condition that would not change the result.
rules.example: Even if it rains, the event will continue.

questions.prompt: ___ the delay, the work was completed.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Despite' takes a noun phrase.
Incorrect: 'Although' would require a clause.
Incorrect: 'Even though' would require a clause.
Incorrect: 'In spite' requires 'of' before a noun phrase.

questions.prompt: ___ the cost rises, we will finish the project.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Even if' presents a hypothetical condition.
Incorrect: 'Even though' suggests a fact, not a hypothetical.
Incorrect: 'Despite' would require a noun phrase.
Incorrect: 'Although' suggests a fact, not a hypothetical.

questions.prompt: Although it was late, ___ working.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'they continued' is the main clause.
Incorrect: 'continued they' has wrong word order.
Incorrect: 'continuing' is not a finite verb.
Incorrect: 'had continued' suggests a different time frame.

questions.prompt: The plan will proceed even if the figures ___ change.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'do' agrees with the plural subject 'figures'.
Incorrect: 'are' would not make sense with 'change'.
Incorrect: 'does' would disagree with the plural subject.
Incorrect: 'will' would be redundant with 'will proceed'.

questions.faultySentence: Although of the risks, they continued.
questions.prompt: Choose a correct concessive form.
choices: Although there were risks, they continued.
In spite of the risks, they continued.
Even with the risks, they continued.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Despite' takes a noun phrase.
Correct: This uses a finite clause with 'Although'.
Correct: 'In spite of' takes a noun phrase.
Correct: This is another concessive form.

questions.faultySentence: Even if it will rain, the match will start.
questions.prompt: Correct the hypothetical condition.
choices: Even if it rains, the match will start.
Even if it rained, the match would start.
Even if it is raining, the match will start.
Even if it rains, the match starts.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'rains' is the present form for future condition.
Correct: This is also possible as a more remote condition.
Correct: This is also possible.
Correct: This is also possible in a different tense.

questions.faultySentence: Despite the road was closed, we arrived.
questions.prompt: Use a clause linker or a noun phrase.
choices: Although the road was closed, we arrived.
Despite the road being closed, we arrived.
Despite the road closed, we arrived.
In spite of the road being closed, we arrived.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Although' takes a finite clause.
Correct: 'Despite' takes a gerund phrase.
Incorrect: 'Despite' cannot take a past participle alone.
Correct: 'In spite of' takes a gerund phrase.

questions.prompt: ___ (although) the task was difficult, it was worthwhile.
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces the contrasting finite clause.

questions.prompt: We will continue even if demand ___ (fall).
questions.explanation: A present form follows 'even if' for a future condition.

questions.prompt: ___ (despite) the warning, the test went ahead.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' takes a noun phrase rather than a finite clause.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct concessive clause sentence.
questions.explanation: The 'although' clause presents an unexpected contrast.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct scalar condition sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Even if' marks a condition that does not affect the result.

topic.title: Academic and Formal Cohesion
topic.summary: Formal linking expressions show addition, contrast, cause, and consequence across academic sentences.

rules.title: Academic linking
rules.explanation: Formal connectors make logical relationships between claims explicit.
rules.example: Furthermore, the second sample confirms the pattern.

rules.title: Resultative cohesion
rules.explanation: 'Therefore', 'thus', and 'consequently' introduce results that follow from preceding information.
rules.example: The sample was small; consequently, the result is tentative.

questions.prompt: The sample was small; ___, it was carefully selected.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'nevertheless' marks a contrast.
Incorrect: 'therefore' would mark a result, not a contrast.
Incorrect: 'however' could work but is more common at start of clause.
Incorrect: 'consequently' would mark a result.

questions.prompt: The evidence was incomplete; ___, no firm conclusion was possible.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'therefore' marks a result.
Incorrect: 'however' would mark a contrast.
Incorrect: 'nevertheless' would mark a contrast.
Incorrect: 'on the other hand' would mark a contrast.

questions.prompt: ___, the findings support the original hypothesis.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Furthermore' adds additional support.
Incorrect: 'However' would mark a contrast.
Incorrect: 'Nevertheless' would mark a contrast.
Incorrect: 'On the other hand' would mark a contrast.

questions.prompt: The device failed and ___ the test was repeated.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'consequently' marks the result of the failure.
Incorrect: 'however' would mark a contrast.
Incorrect: 'nevertheless' would mark a contrast.
Incorrect: 'on the contrary' would mark a contrast.

questions.faultySentence: Despite, the evidence was limited, the claim was useful.
questions.prompt: Replace the incorrect connector.
choices: Although the evidence was limited, the claim was useful.
Despite the evidence being limited, the claim was useful.
In spite of the limited evidence, the claim was useful.
While the evidence was limited, the claim was useful.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Although' introduces a finite clause.
Correct: This is a correct alternative.
Correct: This is a correct alternative.
Correct: This is a correct alternative.

questions.faultySentence: The result was inconsistent, consequently we repeated the test.
questions.prompt: Correct the sentence link punctuation.
choices: The result was inconsistent; consequently, we repeated the test.
The result was inconsistent, and consequently, we repeated the test.
The result was inconsistent; consequently we repeated the test.
The result was inconsistent, so consequently we repeated the test.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Semicolon and comma are correct punctuation.
Correct: This is also correct with a conjunction.
Correct: This is also acceptable.
Correct: This is also acceptable but less formal.

questions.faultySentence: Furthermore of the cost, the method is impractical.
questions.prompt: Use an appropriate formal connector.
choices: In addition to the cost, the method is impractical.
Furthermore, the method is impractical because of the cost.
Moreover, the cost makes the method impractical.
Besides the cost, the method is impractical.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'In addition to' takes a noun phrase.
Correct: This is a correct alternative.
Correct: This is a correct alternative.
Correct: This is a correct alternative.

questions.prompt: The method is inexpensive; ___ (however), it is reliable.
questions.explanation: 'However' marks contrast between the two clauses.

questions.prompt: The controls failed; ___ (consequently), the results were discarded.
questions.explanation: 'Consequently' introduces the result of the failed controls.

questions.prompt: ___ (moreover), the second trial produced the same pattern.
questions.explanation: 'Moreover' adds a further supporting point.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct resultative cohesion sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Consequently' introduces the result after a semicolon.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct academic linking sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Moreover' adds another formal supporting point.

topic.title: Stance, Certainty, and Qualification
topic.summary: Stance expressions qualify claims and distinguish confidence from evidence.

rules.title: Stance noun phrases
rules.explanation: Noun phrases such as 'there is evidence that' express the writer's stance toward a claim.
rules.example: There is strong evidence that the effect is real.

rules.title: Certainty qualification
rules.explanation: Qualifiers calibrate how strongly a claim is presented.
rules.example: The results appear to indicate a modest improvement.

questions.prompt: There is little evidence ___ the treatment works.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'that' introduces the content clause.
Incorrect: 'of' would require a noun phrase.
Incorrect: 'for' would require a noun phrase.
Incorrect: 'about' would require a noun phrase.

questions.prompt: The findings ___ suggest a relationship.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'appear to' is a standard qualification phrase.
Correct: 'seem to' is also a valid qualification.
Correct: 'might' is also a valid modal qualifier.
Correct: 'may' is also a valid modal qualifier.

questions.prompt: There is no reason ___ the result is accidental.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to believe' is the stance infinitive phrase.
Correct: 'for believing' is also possible.
Incorrect: 'that' would introduce a clause but lacks the verb.
Incorrect: 'of' would require a gerund.

questions.prompt: The change is ___ significant.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'potentially' qualifies the significance.
Correct: 'probably' is also a valid qualifier.
Correct: 'possibly' is also a valid qualifier.
Incorrect: 'clearly' suggests certainty, not qualification.

questions.faultySentence: There are strong evidence that the method works.
questions.prompt: Correct the subject-verb agreement in the stance phrase.
choices: There is strong evidence that the method works.
There are strong evidence that the method works.
There is strong evidence for the method working.
There is strong evidence the method works.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'is' agrees with singular 'evidence'.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.
Correct: This is a valid alternative.
Correct: This is also valid without 'that'.

questions.faultySentence: The data definitely appear to perhaps support the claim.
questions.prompt: Reduce the conflicting certainty markers.
choices: The data appear to support the claim.
The data definitely support the claim.
The data perhaps support the claim.
The data appear to support the claim.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Removes the conflicting 'definitely' and 'perhaps'.
Correct: This is a definite claim.
Correct: This is a tentative claim.
Correct: This is the simplest correct version.

questions.faultySentence: There is evidence for the device is safe.
questions.prompt: Complete the stance phrase correctly.
choices: There is evidence that the device is safe.
There is evidence for the device being safe.
There is evidence the device is safe.
There is evidence of the device being safe.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'that' introduces the clause.
Correct: 'for' takes a gerund phrase.
Correct: This is valid without 'that'.
Correct: 'of' takes a gerund phrase.

questions.prompt: There is some evidence ___ (that) the policy helped.
questions.explanation: 'That' introduces the proposition supported by the evidence.

questions.prompt: The results ___ (appear) to be consistent.
questions.explanation: 'Appear to' expresses cautious interpretation.

questions.prompt: The effect is ___ (relatively) small.
questions.explanation: 'Relatively' qualifies the degree of smallness.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct stance phrase sentence.
questions.explanation: 'There is' introduces the stance noun phrase.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct qualification sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Appear to' qualifies the strength of the claim.

topic.title: Lexical Grammar and Valency
topic.summary: Verb valency and light-verb collocations determine which complements and nouns combine naturally.

rules.title: Valency alternation
rules.explanation: Valency describes the complements a verb licenses and how those complements can alternate.
rules.example: The researcher explained the result to the panel.

rules.title: Light-verb collocations
rules.explanation: Light verbs form conventional meanings with abstract nouns, such as 'make a decision'.
rules.example: The committee made a decision.

questions.prompt: The lecturer explained the rule ___ the class.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to' introduces the recipient of the explanation.
Incorrect: 'for' would suggest the explanation was on behalf of someone.
Incorrect: 'at' is not used with 'explain'.
Incorrect: 'with' suggests accompaniment, not recipient.

questions.prompt: The panel ___ a decision after lunch.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'made a decision' is the standard collocation.
Incorrect: 'did a decision' is not a standard collocation.
Incorrect: 'created a decision' is not idiomatic.
Incorrect: 'formed a decision' is less common and more formal.

questions.prompt: They discussed ___ the proposal.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'discuss' takes a direct object.
Incorrect: 'discuss about' is not grammatically correct.
Incorrect: 'discuss on' is not grammatically correct.
Incorrect: 'discuss over' is not grammatically correct.

questions.prompt: We need to ___ progress quickly.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'make progress' is the standard collocation.
Incorrect: 'do progress' is not a standard collocation.
Incorrect: 'take progress' is not a standard collocation.
Incorrect: 'have progress' is not a standard collocation.

questions.faultySentence: She explained us the procedure.
questions.prompt: Use the correct valency pattern.
choices: She explained the procedure to us.
She explained the procedure to us.
She explained to us the procedure.
She explained the procedure for us.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'explain' takes the thing before the recipient.
Correct: This is also correct.
Correct: This is also correct.
Incorrect: 'for us' changes the meaning.

questions.faultySentence: The team did a decision yesterday.
questions.prompt: Replace the incorrect light verb.
choices: The team made a decision yesterday.
The team made a decision yesterday.
The team reached a decision yesterday.
The team came to a decision yesterday.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'made a decision' is the standard collocation.
Correct: This is the standard form.
Correct: 'reached a decision' is also valid.
Correct: 'came to a decision' is also valid.

questions.faultySentence: They suggested us to postpone the launch.
questions.prompt: Use the appropriate suggestion complement.
choices: They suggested that we postpone the launch.
They suggested we postpone the launch.
They suggested to us that we postpone the launch.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'suggested that' is the standard pattern.
Correct: This is also correct with the subjunctive.
Correct: This is also correct.
Correct: This is also correct.

questions.prompt: The guide explained the route ___ (to) the visitors.
questions.explanation: 'To' introduces the recipient of an explanation.

questions.prompt: The researchers ___ (take) measures to reduce risk.
questions.explanation: 'Take measures' is the conventional collocation.

questions.prompt: The new policy will ___ (make) a difference.
questions.explanation: 'Make a difference' is a fixed light-verb combination.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct valency pattern sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Explain' takes the explained thing before the recipient with 'to'.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct light-verb collocation sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Make a difference' is the conventional collocation.

topic.title: Register, Variation, and Editing
topic.summary: Editing choices distinguish standard formal usage from informal or regionally variable alternatives.

rules.title: Standard edited English
rules.explanation: Formal edited prose follows conventions that improve clarity and acceptability across audiences.
rules.example: The committee has not yet reached a decision.

rules.title: Register and variant choice
rules.explanation: A form can be grammatical yet unsuitable for a formal context or a particular audience.
rules.example: The findings were obtained from three sites.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is most suitable for a formal report?
choices: The committee has not reached a decision.
The committee has not reached no decision.
choiceExplanations: Correct: This is formal and grammatically correct.
Incorrect: 'hasn't' is a contraction, less formal.
Incorrect: 'ain't' is non-standard.
Incorrect: This has a double negative.

questions.prompt: Choose the formal alternative to 'a lot of evidence'.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'substantial' is formal.
Correct: 'much' is formal but less descriptive.
Correct: 'ample' is formal.
Correct: 'considerable' is formal.

questions.prompt: The report was written ___ clear English.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'in' is the standard preposition.
Incorrect: 'with' suggests accompaniment.
Incorrect: 'using' changes the structure.
Incorrect: 'by' suggests agent, not language.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is suitable for a cautious academic claim?
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'may indicate' is cautious.
Incorrect: 'show' is more definite.
Incorrect: 'prove' is too strong.
Incorrect: 'demonstrate' is more definite.

questions.faultySentence: The report do not contain no references.
questions.prompt: Edit the double negative and subject-verb agreement.
choices: The report does not contain any references.
The report does not contain references.
The report does not contain no references.
choiceExplanations: Correct: Corrects agreement and double negative.
Correct: This is also correct.
Correct: This is also correct.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.

questions.prompt: Replace the informal overstatement.
choices: The results may support the theory.
The results appear to support the theory.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'may support' is appropriately cautious.
Correct: 'suggest' is also cautious.
Correct: 'appear to support' is also cautious.
Correct: 'indicate' is also acceptable.

questions.prompt: Use the standard count-noun form.
choices: We have fewer errors in the revised version.
We have less errors in the revised version.
We have fewer error in the revised version.
We have less error in the revised version.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'fewer' is used with count nouns.
Incorrect: This repeats the error.

questions.explanation: 'Substantial' is a formal adjective for a considerable amount.

questions.prompt: The results ___ (may) indicate a difference.
questions.explanation: 'May' presents a cautious formal claim.

questions.explanation: 'Fewer' modifies the countable plural noun 'errors'.

questions.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct formal sentence.

topic.title: Advanced Grammar Consolidation
topic.summary: This final level combines advanced clause structure, cohesion, stance, valency, and register in extended contexts.

rules.title: Advanced grammar consolidation
rules.explanation: Advanced grammar choices work together: structure, cohesion, stance, and register must fit the intended meaning.
rules.example: Although the evidence was limited, the results appear to support the conclusion.

questions.prompt: ___ the evidence was limited, the conclusion remained plausible.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'Although' introduces a finite clause.
Incorrect: 'Despite' requires a noun phrase.
Incorrect: 'Even if' would suggest a hypothetical.

questions.prompt: The results ___ indicate a small improvement.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'appear to' is a formal qualification.
Correct: 'seem to' is also a valid qualifier.
Correct: 'may' is also a valid modal qualifier.
Correct: 'might' is also a valid modal qualifier.

questions.prompt: The adviser explained the change ___ the committee.
choiceExplanations: Correct: 'to' introduces the recipient.

Incorrect: 'with' would suggest accompaniment.
